newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW-German economists on UK poll result.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-German economists on UK poll result.

text.p: Britain's Tony Blair swept his Labour Party into power in Britain on Friday, ending 18 years of Conservative rule.
Following is a selection of reactions from analysts in Germany to the prospect of a new, left-of-centre British government.
HOLGER SCHMIEDING, ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH IN FRANKFURT
"In general, I don't think it means very much. Labour has turned a bit anti-European recently as well (as the Conservatives), so we'll really have to wait and see how this works out.
"Blair has such a strong mandate now that he can probably do whatever he wants -- but the problem is, we don't quite know what he wants to do.

"Obviously Bonn and Paris are hoping that Blair will be more conciliatory towards Europe, but the question is whether he will be conciliatory not just in tone, but also in substance. For that, we might have to wait a while."
ADOLF ROSENSTOCK, INDUSTRIAL BANK OF JAPAN, FRANKFURT
"Britain's relation with the European Union will be more relaxed -- that should be the biggest benefit. But I doubt we'll see a more positive stance on European monetary union.

"The stance is likely to be less ideologically agressive and I expect a more sober approach which will nevertheless remain at a distance to EMU. But the working relationship is likely to be better than it has been in recent years.

"The new government will have to make a new start in all areas and that will include the relationship with Europe. The new government is likely to be welcomed with open arms in Europe but hopes for a major shift towards Europe are likely to be disappointed."
"From the German point of view, Britain's stance on Europe is unlikely to change much in the foreseeable future.

"Economic conditions are such that Britain does not want to or cannot move in the direction of European monetary union. Britain is in a totally different economic cycle and it would be very difficult for Britain to cut its rates to German levels.
"Politically, I cannot imagine that Tony Blair will want to immediately pick up a hot potato like EMU which is even controversial within the ranks of his own party.

"If people expect Britain to stage a big swing towards EMU they will be disappointed. Labour is likely to be less hostile in its rhetoric regarding some aspects of European integration but there is unlikely to be a big change in substance."
